title: NCKU Mechatronics Lab's CubeSat Fleet: Lilium-3 and Its Electric Propulsion Experiment
subtitle: Nine CubeSats in the "Mechatronics Laboratory" IRIS/Lilium series — focused on Lilium-3's arc thruster and secure-comms payload
hero_note: National Cheng Kung University's Department of Electrical Engineering "Mechatronics Laboratory" has launched a series of IRIS/Lilium CubeSats since 2022. This story presents the fleet's current orbital status using public TLE history retrieved from this system's own database; descriptions of payloads, mission goals, and technical progress are compiled from public reporting, with the full source list on the last page. Public TLEs can only show orbital trends — they cannot independently confirm payload operation, ignition events, or mission details.

sections.title: Introduction: One Lab, Nine Satellites, Four Years of Launches
sections.body: NCKU's Department of Electrical Engineering "Mechatronics Laboratory" focuses its research on two tracks: space technology (LEO and CubeSats) and smart driving. Starting with IRIS-A (launched 2022-01-13), the lab's team has successively sent up IRIS-C/C2, IRIS-F1/F2/F3, and Lilium 1 through 3 — nine CubeSat catalog objects in all, one of Taiwan's densest runs of self-built CubeSat launches over the past four years. Lilium-2 and Lilium-3, launched together on 2025-11-28 (2025-11-29 Taiwan time), represent the newest generation: Lilium-3 carries, as a hosted payload, a secure-communications module built by SATORO Taiwan Inc. (SATORO Space), alongside a vacuum arc thruster developed in-house by the NCKU team — Taiwan's first electric-propulsion experiment conducted in space. This story focuses on the four newest satellites that still produce TLEs and remain trackable today: Lilium-2, Lilium-3, IRIS-F2, and IRIS-F3.

sections.title: ③ Day-by-Day Orbital-Element Trends: Four-Satellite Comparison
sections.body: Day-by-day orbital elements for each satellite from the earliest available TLE (estimated mean-element trends under the SGP4/TLE model, not instantaneous values from a precision ephemeris). Switch tabs to compare semi-major axis, inclination, and RAAN trends across Lilium-2, Lilium-3, IRIS-F2, and IRIS-F3 — all four currently show a slow decay consistent with atmospheric drag, with no clear maneuver signature observed. See the data-provenance notes on the last page for the maneuver-detection method and thresholds.

sections.title: ④ Why Lilium-3 Is This System's Watch Item
sections.body: Lilium-3 carries a vacuum arc thruster developed in-house by the NCKU team, conducting Taiwan's first electric-propulsion experiment in space to validate attitude-adjustment and orbit-change capability in support of collision-avoidance maneuvers and extended mission life; the satellite also carries, as a hosted payload, SATORO Space's secure-communications module, used to build flight heritage. Official public materials use the term "vacuum arc thruster"; subsequent technical-results reporting further distinguishes two variants — the Vacuum Cathodic Arc Thruster (VCAT) and the Vacuum-Arc-Induced Pulsed Plasma Thruster (VAI-PPT) — of which VCAT has completed its flight demonstration aboard Lilium-3. As of June 2026, related reporting indicates the thruster has completed preliminary ignition and continues to accumulate flight heritage. This system runs the same maneuver-detection pipeline on Lilium-3 that it applies to large constellations like Starlink: flagging candidate maneuver events via a semi-major-axis jump threshold between adjacent TLEs (0.5 km for LEO). Re-checking against the TLEs this system holds from April through September 2026, the semi-major axis decays monotonically and gently across the whole period (about −2.3 km over 166 days), with the largest single jump only about 0.05 km — far below the maneuver threshold, and both the pattern and magnitude are consistent with pure atmospheric drag; no orbital-maneuver signal corresponding to the reported preliminary ignition has been observed. This is an honest statement of current status, not a negative conclusion: the arc thruster is a low-thrust technology-demonstration payload, and the thrust and burn duration of a preliminary ignition test are typically well below the noise floor of public TLEs, so failing to detect a maneuver is the expected outcome — it does not mean ignition did not occur. This system will continue monitoring with its existing pipeline; should a larger-scale orbital maneuver occur later, it would in principle be among the earlier sources to catch the signal in this kind of public data.

sections.title: Closing: What Public TLEs Can — and Cannot — Tell You
sections.body: The same public-TLE monitoring pipeline can show a single lab's launch cadence over four years and nine satellites, the current orbital health of the four still-trackable satellites, and ongoing observation of a specific payload such as Lilium-3's arc thruster. But public TLEs remain nothing more than averaged orbital elements from a public LEO catalog: failing to detect a maneuver today does not mean one won't happen later. The tracking gaps in this system's database (Lilium-1, IRIS-A/C/C2/F1, and so on) reflect the extent of this system's own data coverage, not a conclusion about the satellites' actual operational status. The official and media claims cited in this story — payload contents, thruster technical details, ignition progress — have not been independently verified by this system; the full source list appears below.
